scenes.text: A bank's chatbot suddenly starts giving stock tips, or insulting a customer. [1] That would be a disaster. So how do companies keep AI on track? [2] With guardrails. Let's see how they work in real products.
[1] Guardrails are safety checks placed around an AI model. [2] They check what goes in, [3] they check what comes out, [4] and they stop, or fix, anything unsafe or off-topic.

data.definition: Safety checks around an AI model that filter inputs and outputs, keeping it safe and on-topic.

scenes.text: Here's a typical guarded chatbot. [1] The user's message arrives. [2] An input check blocks attacks, like prompt injection, and hides personal data. [3] The model writes a reply, following its system prompt. [4] An output check scans for harmful content, made-up facts, or leaked data. [5] Only then does the safe reply reach the user.

There are three common guardrail types. [1] Topic limits, a bank bot only talks about banking. [2] Content moderation, blocking hate, violence, or self harm content, and sharing help resources. [3] Format checks, making sure answers are valid, like correct JSON for an app, or a real account number format.

Here are real examples. [1] A food delivery bot politely refuses to write your college essay. [2] A health app adds, please consult a doctor, to medical answers. [3] And a banking bot hands off to a human, when a customer is angry, or the question is complex.

Here are four terms. [1] PII, personally identifiable information, like phone numbers, and Aadhaar. [2] Moderation model, a classifier that flags harmful text. [3] Fallback, a safe response when something fails. [4] And human handoff, passing the conversation to a real person.

Here's a common myth. [1] People think a good system prompt is enough to keep the AI safe. [2] Prompts can be tricked, as we saw with jailbreaks. Real products stack several layers, input checks, output checks, and human review.

data.myth: A good system prompt is enough to keep AI safe.
data.fact: Prompts can be tricked. Real products stack layers: input checks, output checks and human review.
